source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: On text editing, learning the library and search net lifted the solve rate from almost nothing to near the best hand-built solver.
numbers: Test on 108 SyGuS 2017 problems, trained on 128 generated tasks. Before learning 3.7% solved in 10 min (mean 235 s). After learning 79.6% (mean 40 s). CVC4 (1 h, 8 CPUs, hand-built libraries per problem) 82.4%. DreamCoder with that budget 84.3%.
limits: One library of generic edit concepts, not one per problem. Compute heavy. Text editing has plenty of shared sub-structure.
agent_relevance: A solved-task library plus a learned guide can make a failing agent competitive, but only where tasks share parts.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder, ablation and baseline section
finding: Both sleep phases matter. Removing the recognition net (dreaming) or library growth (abstraction) lowers held-out solves. Memorise-solutions baselines do worse.
numbers: Full model solved the most held-out tasks in all domains. Mean time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative passed 60% held-out while DreamCoder reached nearly 100%. Library depth correlated with tasks solved at r = 0.79. Training takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs.
limits: Baselines are the authors' re-implementations. Depth-solve correlation is not causal.
agent_relevance: Keep two separate offline jobs: compress solutions into reusable parts, and train the guide on replays. Verbatim memorising is weaker.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder, physics and recursion experiments
finding: From generic map/fold primitives the system rebuilt vector algebra and physics laws. From minimal Lisp primitives it rebuilt a recursive list language, but slowly.
numbers: 60 physics laws and identities: 93% learned after 8 wake/sleep cycles. Lisp bootstrap on 20 problems: all solved after roughly 5 days on 64 CPUs. An earlier origami-style run took about a year of CPU time.
limits: Cost is large. Starting from a minimal base is the hard regime.
agent_relevance: Library growth builds on older entries, so cheap cycles matter for an LLM agent.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: A top-down compression algorithm replaces DreamCoder's refactoring step. It is far faster with comparable library quality.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder's deductive library learner. Test compression 2.55x-11.57x in 0.19-60.16 s on one benchmark set. Robust to early stopping.
limits: Measures compression, not downstream solve rate. Needs a formal DSL.
agent_relevance: The library step can be made cheap. Compression is measurable, so a lesson store could report how much it compresses solved cases.

source: Grand et al. (2024, ICLR) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LLM-guided search plus Stitch compression plus auto-written names and docstrings beat DreamCoder on string editing and scene tasks, and beat the LLM alone clearly on graphics only.
numbers: Mean % test solved (REGEX / CLEVR / LOGO), 3 seeds: DreamCoder 43.93 / 94.50 / 28.53. LLM solver 76.13 / 88.67 / 32.13. LLM solver + search 76.60 / 96.44 / 37.84. LILO 77.07 / 96.76 / 48.95. LILO LOGO std 22.15.
limits: Gains over the LLM-only solver are small on REGEX and CLEVR, with wide seed spread. Codex used.
agent_relevance: Libraries help most where tasks share real structure (graphics) and little elsewhere. Report seed variance.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: AutoDoc ablation and validity of LLM-proposed abstractions
finding: Natural-language names for library items help the LLM use them on some domains, not all. Asking the LLM itself to propose abstractions mostly fails.
numbers: AutoDoc added +9.73 points (REGEX) and +2.27 (CLEVR) over the no-doc condition, +0.00 on LOGO. Only 19.01% (998 of 5250) of LLM-generated abstractions were valid (REGEX 24.93%, CLEVR 24.20%, LOGO 4.93%).
limits: Validity tested in a formal DSL.
agent_relevance: Store lessons with readable names and a usage note. Do not trust a model to propose its own abstractions without a check.

source: Wong et al. (2022) LAPS: leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics
finding: Adding language annotations to the wake-sleep loop raised held-out solves, even with no language at test time.
numbers: % held-out solved, strings / graphics (best run) / scenes: DreamCoder no language 33.4 / 49.55 / 73.9. LAPS + mutual exclusivity + compression 54.60 / 98.19 / 95.9. Graphics seed-mean for that model 81.98 versus 42.64 for DreamCoder. Human-written language train and test: 48.6 / 58.55 / 95.6. No language at test, LAPS library with enumerative search: 33.2 / 62.16 / 93.04.
limits: Synthetic language gives much bigger gains than human language on graphics (98.19 vs 58.55). Best-run numbers overstate typical runs.
agent_relevance: Natural-language descriptions of stored solutions plausibly help retrieval and reuse.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: A gradient-free refactor-verify-prune loop that builds a helper-function bank lifted program accuracy for most LLMs on most datasets.
numbers: Accuracy primitive -> ReGAL, 3 seeds: CodeLlama-13B LOGO 45.6 -> 57.1, Date 42.8 -> 68.9, TextCraft 18.8 -> 26.9. CodeLlama-7B MATH 6.8 -> 17.6. GPT-3.5 LOGO 36.9 -> 49.3, MATH 43.2 -> 55.4, Date 88.9 -> 90.2.
limits: Not uniform. CodeLlama-7B LOGO 34.5 -> 34.5 (no gain). Lemur-70B MATH 14.0 -> 13.1 (drop). CodeLlama-13B TabMWP 29.1 -> 27.9. Baseline had the same 10 in-context examples.
agent_relevance: Library help depends on model and domain. Test with and without the store per task family.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL: ablations, distribution shift, limits
finding: Each part of the loop contributes. Retrials and pruning matter most. Under distribution shift the gain shrinks. More pruning on new data helps.
numbers: Ablations on CodeLlama-13B, 3 seeds: removing any part dropped accuracy. Under shift ReGAL beat the primitive baseline by 3.6%. Pruning an existing bank added 3.5%. Learning new abstractions on unseen dev data added 2.3%. Total 9.4% over baseline.
limits: Authors state not every domain has reusable abstractions, and verification-based pruning finds none in dynamic environments. Learned abstractions differ from human ones.
agent_relevance: Prune the store on fresh data. Expect nothing where tasks do not share parts.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes
finding: Using, growing and periodically trimming a toolbox gave simpler, more accurate programs than a no-library baseline and than creating one function per instance.
numbers: 11 datasets, CodeLlama-7B. Toolboxes 79-98% smaller. Humans verified 31% faster and 13% more accurately. Instance-level function creation hurt on visual QA: correctness 0.21 below the primitive baseline.
limits: Later questioned by b13 and b14. Much of the benefit may come from sampling more.
agent_relevance: Unbounded lesson growth distracts the model. Trimming is needed.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: comparison with CRAFT and Creator using GPT-4
finding: Without supervision TroVE matched or beat tool-creation baselines with far smaller libraries.
numbers: Accuracy / library size on three tasks (their Table 3): TroVE 0.72/16, 0.92/38, 0.44/8. CRAFT 0.68/282, 0.88/181, 0.45/525. Creator 0.65/875, 0.81/4595, 0.34. LATM 0.30, 0.09, 0.29. TroVE reports CRAFT near random with CodeLlama.
limits: Authors' own comparison with different pipelines.
agent_relevance: Smaller curated stores can do as well as huge ones.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library (LEGO-Prover)
finding: In LEGO-Prover almost no learned lemma is reused. A version that cannot reuse lemmas performs about the same. Self-correction through the request database is the likelier driver.
numbers: LEGO-Prover learned over 20,000 lemmas. Only 1,233 (6%) reached the prover prompt. Exactly one lemma was reused, once, verbatim. No lemma name appeared in 3 or more solutions. Problems solved: valid+GPT 127, valid+Human 135, test+GPT 111, test+Human 122.
limits: Log analysis plus an ablation on a miniF2F subset. Indirect reuse as examples is not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Warning: a library that is not reused is not why the agent improved. Measure reuse directly.

source: Berlot-Attwell et al. (2024) analysis of TroVE on MATH
finding: TroVE's libraries were tiny and almost never reused. An ablation with no library and the same 15 attempts matched or beat it on most splits.
numbers: 15 learned functions in total, covering 3 of 7 MATH splits. 3 successful reuses in 3,201 test questions. Ablation without IMPORT mode exceeded baseline on 3 of 4 splits tested, significant on two. Authors: typically TroVE's library learning degrades performance.
limits: CodeLlama-7B only. Import-statement libraries can help slightly in some domains.
agent_relevance: Gains credited to libraries may be self-consistency from sampling more. Control for sample count.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past episodes and supplying them to a web agent raised success on WebArena and Mind2Web.
numbers: WebArena: +12.0 absolute points, 51.1% relative over BrowserGym baseline. Gains of 11.8-30.7 points on each of 5 websites. Beat human-written-workflow method SteP by 7.6% relative. Mind2Web step success +24.6% relative. Margin over baselines grew from 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test distance widened.
limits: Online induction learns from the agent's own earlier outputs without gold labels.
agent_relevance: A wake-then-abstract step on an agent log. Workflows in memory work.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory: workflows as actions
finding: Adding workflows as callable actions barely helped. Agents rarely call them.
numbers: Step success +1.3 points. Overall success unchanged at 3.2 (base AWM). Workflow actions called in only 18.5% of tasks.
limits: Side study of a variant.
agent_relevance: Show past routines as context, not as new tools.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: A growing code skill library and an automatic curriculum let a GPT-4 agent keep improving in Minecraft. Without the library progress flattens.
numbers: Replacing the curriculum with a random one cut discovered items by 93%. Without the skill library the agent plateaus in later stages. Giving AutoGPT the skill library let it solve a tech-tree item in 1 of 3 runs (39 iterations) where plain AutoGPT had 0 of 3.
limits: Ablation shown as curves with few seeds. GPT-4 only. Skills are verified by execution.
agent_relevance: Verified, executable skills with a curriculum matter more late in a run than early.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute: beyond inference scaling at test-time
finding: Letting a model think about a context before the question arrives cuts test-time compute and can raise accuracy.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. Scaling sleep-time compute added up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Sharing it across several questions on one context cut cost per query 2.5x. Beat pass@k at equal test-time tokens.
limits: Datasets built by splitting problems into context and question. More parallel sleep generations did not always help: 5 beat 10 on GSM.
agent_relevance: The closest modern LLM form of offline replay: precompute inferences over stored context before queries.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute: when it works
finding: The benefit depends on how predictable the query is from the context.
numbers: Predictability was measured as the log-probability of the question given the context under Llama2-70B. More predictable questions gained most. Largest gains on harder tasks with stronger models (P2 with gpt-4o).
limits: Correlational. The software-engineering case study was qualitative.
agent_relevance: Offline passes help only if future questions can be anticipated.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2025) SOAR: self-improving LMs for evolutionary program synthesis on ARC-AGI
finding: Alternating search (wake) with fine-tuning on hindsight-relabelled attempts (sleep) lifted ARC scores across model sizes.
numbers: ARC-train extra problems solved: +27% (7B), +24% (14B), +20% (32B), +19% (72B). ARC-test: 7B 14.25% -> 36.25%, 14B 19.87% -> 42.75%, 32B 25.25% -> 44.37%, 72B 25.62% -> 44.87%, Mistral-Large-2 26.25% -> 45.5%. Majority vote of all models 52.00%, oracle 57.25%. Joint sample-and-refine fine-tuning beat task-specific fine-tuning.
limits: Needs weight updates, so not scaffold-only. Gains shrink each iteration. Test-time training used test inputs without labels.
agent_relevance: Replaying failed attempts as new pairs works but needs training. A scaffold could only imitate it with stored examples.

source: Pourcel et al. (2025) SOAR: plateau analysis
finding: Search alone plateaus with model size and with search budget. The learning phase lifts the ceiling.
numbers: Without learning, curves flatten beyond 32B and saturate after about 5.2k attempts. Two test-time training iterations added about 5 points on ARC-test. Authors note gains diminish over iterations.
limits: Whether the limit is intrinsic is open (authors).
agent_relevance: More sampling does not replace a learned update between rounds.

source: Bornschein and Bengio (2015) Reweighted wake-sleep
finding: Reading wake-sleep as importance sampling gives better gradient estimates when several samples are drawn from the recognition net.
numbers: Better likelihoods on sigmoidal belief network experiments with the reweighted procedure. The paper says the original wake-sleep justification was questioned because it optimises a KL divergence in the wrong direction.
limits: Early small-network setting. A sigmoid belief net was judged too weak for the recognition layer.
agent_relevance: Wake-sleep is statistically weak when the guide is poor. Keep a check on the guide.

source: Le, Kosiorek, Siddharth, Teh, Wood (2019) Revisiting reweighted wake-sleep for models with stochastic control flow
finding: Reweighted wake-sleep beat variational methods for models with discrete branching, and it has a specific failure mode.
numbers: RWS learned better models and inference nets than IWAE-style objectives in their tests. Failure: a local optimum where the model's support (values 0-9) is never widened because it is trained only on its own guide's samples. Wake-sleep and wake-wake were more affected than VIMCO variants.
limits: Shown under an adverse initialisation. Authors hypothesise alternating objectives suffer more.
agent_relevance: Training the store only on what the current guide proposes can lock in blind spots. Add outside examples.

source: Shin, Lee, Kim, Kim (2017) Continual learning with deep generative replay
finding: A generator that replays earlier tasks' samples to a solver prevents catastrophic forgetting without storing the data.
numbers: Chain of scholar models on MNIST, solver accuracy 98.81, 98.64, 98.58, 98.53, 98.56% across five solvers. Sequential training on the solver alone forgot. Replaying random noise did not help. Replaying generated samples did.
limits: Small image tasks. Generator quality limits replay.
agent_relevance: Replaying generated cases can stand in for stored raw cases at a small accuracy cost.

source: van de Ven and Tolias (2019) Three scenarios for continual learning
finding: Replay was the only family that worked when task identity is unknown. Regularisation failed.
numbers: Split MNIST, 20 seeds, Domain-IL / Class-IL accuracy: none 59.21 / 19.90. EWC 63.95 / 20.01. LwF 71.50 / 23.85. DGR 95.72 / 90.79. DGR+distill 96.83 / 91.79. iCaRL 94.57 (Class-IL). Upper bound 98.42 / 97.94.
limits: MNIST only. Task-IL was easy for all methods (above 98%).
agent_relevance: Replay beats constraints on the hard version of the problem.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLMs with self-synthesized rehearsal
finding: An LLM can write its own rehearsal data from few-shot prompts and nearly match real-data rehearsal.
numbers: Llama-2-7b, 10 SuperNI tasks, average result: SSR 63.23, no rehearsal 17.33, 1% random real replay 60.64, 10% 61.49, multitask upper bound 64.69. Forward transfer on 5 tasks: SSR 27.70 versus 27.99 for 10% random replay.
limits: Falls short of 10% real replay on forward transfer. 7B models only.
agent_relevance: Self-generated rehearsal items are enough to hold older skills. Cheap for a lesson store.

source: Krishnan, Tadros, Ramyaa, Bazhenov (2019) Biologically inspired sleep algorithm for artificial neural networks
finding: A spiking sleep phase with local learning rules recovered tasks lost to forgetting and helped noise robustness.
numbers: In a toy task, after sleep both task 1 and task 2 reached 100% accuracy. Sleep gave forward transfer about 50% of the time on unseen tasks.
limits: Small networks. Needs ANN-to-SNN conversion. Benefit appeared only some of the time.
agent_relevance: Biology-style replay can be tested but little transfers to a text scaffold.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) CRAFT: customizing LLMs by creating and retrieving from specialized toolsets
finding: CRAFT builds a deduplicated toolset from validated GPT-4 solutions and retrieves from it at test time. Only the abstract and TroVE's report of it were read.
numbers: TroVE lists CRAFT at 0.68/282, 0.88/181, 0.45/525 (accuracy / toolset size) with GPT-4. TroVE reports CRAFT near random with CodeLlama.
limits: Second-hand figures. Not read in full.
agent_relevance: Treat as an unconfirmed comparison point.
